card.hook: Seven streams tumble down a dark mountainside side by side, and straight across the fjord a single lonely waterfall watches them. Legend says he's flirting, so you're basically photographing a dance.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 450 m east of the Seven Sisters Waterfall, and face west. Stay safe and keep an eye on your surroundings.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the full height of the falls with a bit of fjord. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the seven streams. Skip 0.5x here, because it makes the falls look small and far away.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bright part of the water, then slide the brightness down a little so the white streams keep their detail.
card.best_time: Water flow changes, so check conditions on the day. One page says the falls are fullest from late May to July. Light and weather also change how clearly the seven streams show against the rock.
card.selfie_here: Try the Ørnesvingen viewpoint (Eagle Bend), the viewing platform above the fjord on Eagle Road, where visitors pose with the Seven Sisters behind them. Use the front camera at 1x and put the falls over your shoulder. They look distant from up there, so treat them as a scenic backdrop.
card.rules_and_safety: The falls are a natural landmark in a World Heritage area, so stay aware of your surroundings while you take photos.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot, then one close-up, and count all seven streams. Bonus points if you spot The Suitor across the water.
card.good_to_know: The whole fall is about 410 metres tall, and the tallest of the seven streams drops about 250 metres in free fall. It's the 39th tallest waterfall in Norway and sits within the West Norwegian Fjords World Heritage Site. The falls lie just south of the old Knivsflå farm, across the fjord from the old Skageflå farm.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 450 m east of the Seven Sisters Waterfall, and face west. Stay safe and keep an eye on your surroundings.

selfie_spots.why: Visitors are photographed here with the Seven Sisters behind them, though the falls look distant from this height.

selfie_research.notes: Only one selfie spot is supported by the pages I found: the sources name Ørnesvingen as a place where people photograph with the falls behind them, but none says the falls fill a selfie frame there, and the falls look distant from the platform. Flydalsjuvet is named as a closer viewpoint with spray and mist, but no page describes a selfie there, so I left it out. The Skageflå spot is a roughly 6 km hike from Geiranger village, or a boat transfer to the shoreline followed by a shorter climb; the pages do not say the spot is easy to find without a guide or map. The ask-someone spot is my reading of a photographer's composition, not a stated instruction for a passer-by. Visibility of the falls depends on water levels, and the falls are fullest from late May to July according to one page. No page I found states rules about selfie sticks or tripods, and none names a safety point specific to these spots.

card.hook: Most people meet Geirangerfjord over a roadside railing, but you're going to earn this one with a 40 to 60 minute uphill walk. At the top, an abandoned mountain farm sits right in front of the Seven Sisters waterfall, and the climb tends to keep the crowds down.
card.stand_here: Stand at Skageflå, on the trail right beside the old farm buildings. Face the fjord, which lies ahead of you to the north, and look for the angle where the buildings are in front and the Seven Sisters are behind.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to get the farm, the fjord and the waterfall all in one shot. Then try 1x for a calmer, less stretched look, and 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the Seven Sisters on their own.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the farm on the lower third, then tap the fjord and slide it a touch darker so the white water of the falls keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Go between May and July, when the falls carry more water and look their best. Morning or late afternoon gives you softer light.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Ørnesvingen (Eagle Bend) observation deck at the top of the Ørnevegen hairpin bends. Use the front camera (try 0.5x) and keep the fjord and the Seven Sisters over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: At the Ørnesvingen deck, ask a passer-by to stand on the deck while you stand near the railing with the fjord and the Seven Sisters behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The rock above the fjord at Flydalsjuvet is unfenced with a huge drop, so stay back from the edge and skip it when it's wet or icy. At Skageflå, check local information for current trail conditions and respect the old buildings.
card.challenge: Can you get the whole farm roof, a bit of fjord and at least one waterfall in the same shot without tilting your phone?
card.good_to_know: Geirangerfjord is a 15-kilometre branch of the Sunnylvsfjorden and has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2005, together with the Nærøyfjorden. The Seven Sisters face another waterfall across the fjord, called the Suitor. Skageflå is one of several farms along the fjord that people have partly restored, and it's the one you can reach on foot from Geiranger.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Skageflå, on the trail right beside the old farm buildings. Face the fjord, which lies ahead of you to the north, and look for the angle where the buildings are in front and the Seven Sisters are behind.

selfie_spots.why: The rock juts out over the fjord, so a selfie taken there puts the fjord and the village of Geiranger behind you, though the view is less expansive than at the main lookouts.

selfie_research.safety: The rock above the fjord at Flydalsjuvet is unfenced with a huge drop, so stay back from the edge and avoid visiting when it is wet or icy.
selfie_research.notes: Only the Flydalsjuvet rock spot is a true 'with the landmark behind' selfie; it is unofficial, not signposted, and requires stepping over a fence, so it is a site the authorities do not promote. The Roads & Rivers page calls the rock spot 'Queens Chair' on Google Maps, but another source uses that name for a separate wooden chair on the lower plateau, so check the name before you navigate. The Walk My World and Roads & Rivers pages describe the same spot differently: one says the photographer stands on the rock, the other says the visitor walks along the precipice to the fence. The Norwegian Routes page places Flydalsjuvet 'just behind' Geiranger, but the other sources put it about 4 to 6 km away on Route 63, so do not rely on walking distance. No page I found states any rule on selfie sticks or tripods, and the drone-rules guide was not readable in the results, so no drone rule is reported. The given position (62.121, 7.129) is near Geiranger village, while both spots are a short drive away.

card.hook: Steep mountain walls drop straight into the water here, and the harbour and village tuck neatly in between. You get the whole scene in one frame, so there's no fiddly framing needed.
card.stand_here: Stand about 150 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map near Ørnevegen, and face east. Take in the whole scene first, then move in for details.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the village, harbour and both mountain walls. Switch to 1x for a more natural view, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out details in the distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and, if there's water in your shot, put the waterline on the lower third line so the mountains and sky get the rest of the frame.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light. The tourist season runs from May to early September, and it gets busy in summer.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Fjord Seat (Fjordsetet), the big wooden chair on the lower platform at Flydalsjuvet viewpoint. Sit in it, use the front camera at 0.5x, and let the fjord and village spread out behind you.
card.ask_someone: At Ørnesvingen (Eagle Bend), the viewing platform at the upper hairpin of the Eagle Road, ask a passer-by to stand on the platform and frame you with the village and fjord spread below.
card.rules_and_safety: At Flydalsjuvet the rock photo spot is unfenced above a huge drop, so stay back from the edge and skip it when it's wet or icy. Check the official site for any restrictions around the port or cruise terminal. Ørnesvingen is about 8 km from the village centre and its parking is limited.
card.challenge: Take one shot with a cruise ship for scale against the mountains and one without, then pick your favourite.
card.good_to_know: Geiranger is a small village of 215 people (2023), but between 140 and 180 cruise ships call during the four-month season. The floating Seawalk pier, built in 2013, is 236 metres long. The area is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, so keep the wider view in a few shots.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 150 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map near Ørnevegen, and face east. Take in the whole scene first, then move in for details.

selfie_spots.why: Sitting in the chair puts you above the fjord with the village spread out in the view, which gives a classic Geiranger backdrop.

selfie_research.safety: At Flydalsjuvet, the rock photo spot is unfenced above a huge drop, so stay back from the edge and avoid visiting when it is wet or icy and the rock is slippery.
selfie_research.notes: The Fjord Seat and the Ørnesvingen platform are both named viewpoints but the sources do not state exactly which way the sitter faces, so check the orientation on site. The Geiranger swing is supported by one blog post only, and the sources do not confirm the village is in frame behind it, so it is the weaker of the two selfie spots. Ørnesvingen is about 8 km from the village centre and parking there is limited. The sources give no specific photo spot on the harbour itself, and no page I found mentions selfie-stick or tripod rules.

card.hook: Picture a few tiny buildings perched on a ledge, with a giant rock wall behind them and a very long drop to the fjord below. That's Skageflå, and it makes you wonder who thought this was a good place to keep goats.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 530 m west of the subject, and face east. You'll see the farm on its ledge on the mountainside above the fjord.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 2x or 5x to pick the farm out from the mountainside (higher zooms depend on your phone). Then try 1x for a wider shot where the farm looks small against the cliffs. Use 0.5x only if you want the sweep of the fjord walls, because the farm will be tiny.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the farm on one of the crossing points rather than in the middle, with plenty of rock above and slope below so everyone can see how steep it is.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day, because haze or low cloud will hide a faraway farm. Soft light from the side shows more detail in the buildings than flat midday light does.
card.selfie_here: At the farm, try the little doghouse among the old buildings, where sunlight comes through the trees above it. Use the front camera and hold it a bit out so the buildings fill in around you. For a fjord selfie, walk out onto the grass just below the farm and turn your back to the fjord. You'll get the fjord behind you, but the farm will be behind the camera, not behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to photograph you in the patch of weeds just off the trail on the right-hand side of the farm, with the huts in the foreground and the Seven Sisters waterfalls behind.
card.rules_and_safety: The hike has several steep, narrow and exposed sections, and one guide says it isn't suitable for children or anyone afraid of heights. Check the official site or the boat and tour operators before you go.
card.challenge: Take two shots: one zoomed in on the buildings, then one wide with the fjord, and see if a friend can guess how far apart they were taken.
card.good_to_know: People lived at Skageflå from the Middle Ages until 1916. It was once one of the richer goat farms around Geiranger, with two or three mountain pastures for its animals. A rock slide in 1873 destroyed much of the cultivated land, and the farm sits about 250 metres above the fjord.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 530 m west of the subject, and face east. You'll see the farm on its ledge on the mountainside above the fjord.

selfie_spots.detail: on the grass just below the farm buildings, walking out toward the cliff top
selfie_spots.why: This is the fjord-facing edge that gives the best fjord views, though the farm ends up behind the camera rather than behind the visitor.

selfie_research.notes: No page places a visitor with Skageflå literally behind them, so both selfie spots are the closest matches the pages give; the first puts the fjord behind the visitor. The blog recommends the weeds spot as a photo point for the farm but does not say which way the camera should face. No page states selfie stick or tripod rules. card.hook: Count the sides: this little white church has eight, and a tiny tower perched on the roof like a hat. It's the easiest building in Geiranger to spot, and it sits neatly against the steep slopes.
card.stand_here: Head to the phone icon near Mjelkesletta, about 25 m south-east of the church. Face north-west and the whole eight-sided building fits in your frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole church with a bit of the village around it. Switch to 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for the tower and roofline. If you step in close, try 0.5x to catch the whole front.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so the church doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light and fewer people. Midday sun can make those white walls glare, so you may get a washed-out church.
card.selfie_here: Try the churchyard, on the grass at the front of the church, where one reviewer says the view over the fjord and landscape is amazing. Use the front camera at 0.5x so the fjord fills the frame behind you.
card.ask_someone: Try the gate on the main road through Geiranger (route 63), which one page calls the best place for a view of the church, and ask someone to take your photo with the church in the background.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working parish church, so the grounds and any entry may depend on church times or services. Check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot with the doorway empty and one with visitors walking past, then pick your favourite.
card.good_to_know: Architect Hans Klipe designed the church, and it was finished in 1842. It seats about 124 people and is only about 21 m across, which is why it fits in one frame so easily. Records of a church on this spot go back to 1589, and the previous one burned down in 1841.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the phone icon near Mjelkesletta, about 25 m south-east of the church. Face north-west and the whole eight-sided building fits in your frame.

selfie_spots.name: Churchyard in front of Geiranger Church
selfie_spots.detail: on the grass at the front of the church, facing out over the fjord and the landscape below
selfie_spots.why: A reviewer says the view of the surrounding landscape is amazing from the front of the church, so the fjord can fill the frame behind you.
